The brain is actually two organs
Neuroscience has long assumed that the human brain develops from a single progenitor cell, but a new study led by Stanford Medicine suggests otherwise. The team found that the brain is actually composed of two distinct organs — one governing automatic survival functions like breathing and heartbeat, and another responsible for higher-order thinking — that evolved separately and only later became physically joined.
By examining mouse embryos, the researchers identified two separate cell populations that never overlap. One becomes the forebrain and midbrain and the other is the hindbrain, and differences in how DNA is packaged in each cell cause different developmental fates.
Based on this insight, the team successfully grew functional human hindbrain motor neurons in a lab dish for the first time, which has been an obstacle for research into diseases like ALS and spinal muscular atrophy.
“Previous attempts to make hindbrain neurons likely tried to coax forebrain and midbrain progenitors into hindbrain cells, which our study shows is not possible,” said M.D. and Ph.D. student Rayyan Jokhai, a co-first author on the study.
The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, will provide new possibilities for studying brain stem disorders that have been difficult to model in the lab.
Extreme heat
As heat waves grow longer and more frequent worldwide, Stanford researchers across engineering, medicine and earth sciences are testing practical ways to keep people and buildings cool.
In Makassar, Indonesia, where roughly 40% of residents live in informal settlements without air conditioning, a team led by Rishee Jain, associate professor of civil and environmental engineering, and John Openshaw, assistant professor of infectious diseases, is painting metal rooftops with reflective white paint, a low-cost intervention that can lower indoor temperatures by up to 5 degrees Fahrenheit. The team is also outfitting volunteers with wearable sensors to measure heart rate and sleep patterns, comparing results between painted and unpainted homes to build a case for wider adoption.
“Big interventions can take decades to bring into place, and we don’t have that time. People are suffering from events now,” Openshaw said.
Other researchers are tackling the problem from different angles. In San Francisco, Gregory Deierlein, John A. Blume Professor in the School of Engineering, is working with the city to model how buildings and residents would fare across combined hazards like heat waves and earthquakes, aiming to bundle solutions instead of addressing risks separately.
Catherine Gorlé, associate professor of civil and environmental engineering, is studying how natural ventilation and urban greenery can cool buildings and city blocks, pointing to Medellín, Colombia’s tree-planting campaign, which was linked to an average temperature drop of 2 degrees Celsius over three years.
“There is a lot of opportunity to bring green spaces and blue spaces back into cities, not only to make them in general nicer to live in, but also more comfortable during heat waves,” Gorlé said.
All of these research efforts reflect a push at Stanford to move quickly on practical and effective solutions as extreme heat becomes an unavoidable part of life in cities worldwide.
Tracking toxic metals in wildfire smoke
Stanford researchers are building systems to detect a danger in wildfire smoke that current air quality monitoring misses: toxic metals that are released when extreme heat transforms naturally occurring soil minerals into airborne particles.
The project, called SmokeCast, started with professor of earth system science Scott Fendorf’s investigation into the 2019 Kincade Fire, which showed that a fire’s location determines how much toxic metal ends up in its smoke.
This summer, the team tested a prototype device on a firetruck dispatched to a Colorado wildfire. The device is a briefcase-sized array of air filters and satellite sensors which provided the team with real-time data on temperature, humidity and gases like carbon monoxide, while also estimating the odds that nearby soils would release toxic metals.
Existing measures like the EPA’s Air Quality Index track fine particle concentration but not chemical composition. “It doesn’t tell you anything about chemistry, and that is a huge gap,” said Alexander Honeyman, postdoctoral scholar in Fendorf’s research group.
With backing from the Stanford Sustainability Accelerator, the team hopes to outfit more firetrucks with the sensors and eventually offer a public smoke-toxicity forecast in the coming years.

It’s a question that many homeowners will be asking after seeing the damage that roots do, as they scour the area for any drops of moisture. Here’s the word from Mainmark;
As the recent prolonged hot and dry weather has increased the risk of tree-related subsidence, Mainmark UK is urging homeowners not to resort to tree removal without first seeking expert advice. Instead, the ground engineering specialist is advocating sustainable solutions that protect both properties and the environment.
The likes of cracked walls, sloping or sinking floors, or jamming doors or windows are all tell-tale signs of tree-related subsidence, where the ground beneath a building or structure starts to sink. Subsidence is an increasing risk for homeowners, particularly those living on shrinkable clay soils near large water-demanding trees like oak, poplar or willow.
Trees play an important role in providing shade, are valuable habitats for wildlife and help tackle climate change by absorbing carbon dioxide and filtering pollutants from the air. Greater consideration needs to be placed on retaining and managing existing trees, as areas with more trees and green spaces are up to 5°C cooler.
Freya Chapman, Residential Lead at Mainmark UK, said: “Following this year’s hotter months, we are anticipating a significant surge of tree-related subsidence. This is caused by tree roots extracting water from the soil faster than it can be replenished (when moisture is scarce). This, in turn, can cause the dissociated clay soil to dry and shrink at a fast rate, resulting in ground movement and instability for the foundations of homes.
“As wetter conditions return during Autumn and if the trees have been removed then the area can heave during the recovery of the clay soils Traditionally, homes at the highest risk of subsidence will be those located in areas with largely clay soil, including London and the home counties, Essex and the South East.”
Mainmark UK is encouraging homeowners experiencing signs of subsidence to seek expert assessment before considering tree removal.
Some traditional remediation methods can be more invasive and may affect root systems or natural water movement within the soil. A less invasive alternative is a root barrier solution containing copper which creates a shield underground to redirect tree root growth. Copper being the only compound that tree roots naturally divert away from.
Freya continued: “We need to better educate homeowners on the sustainable treatment of trees causing subsidence. We can help homeowners mitigate subsidence claims and protect the surrounding vegetation and our trees using the latest technologies non-disruptively and cost-effectively.”
Alongside copper root barriers, injecting a specialised engineered resin underneath a home’s foundations or concrete slabs can help strengthen and re-level the ground. The resin expands, compacting weak soils, filling voids and lifting the structure back to level to benefit both the homeowner and the natural environment.
Freya added: “Recently, we were involved in a project in Wales to address a long-standing issue of subsidence at the property. Four large trees were causing issues to the side and rear of a bungalow. In a matter of hours, we installed a root barrier and injected resin to successfully protect the property from further movement.”
Mainmark UK is a member of the Subsidence Forum Committee, which brings together experts and the company works collaboratively with arborists, insurers and civil engineers and campaigns for the development of textile-based root barriers using copper.

Bangkok launches new effort to address health impacts of extreme heat
Heat, health and vulnerability data will identify high-risk communities and guide targeted heat-health measures
PUBLISHED : 22 Sep 2026 at 10:40
The Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA) has announced that the city will begin development of its Integrated and Evidence-Based Heat–Health Action Plan as part of Bangkok’s work with the Partnership for Healthy Cities—a global network of more than 70 cities committed to saving lives by preventing noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) and injuries.
The initiative, launched in collaboration with the Asian Institute of Technology (AIT), will use scientific evidence to identify the neighborhoods where heat poses the greatest health risks, who is most vulnerable and what measures can better protect residents.
Dr Lertluck Leelaruangsang, Deputy Permanent Secretary of the BMA, said, “Extreme heat is not only a climate issue; it has direct impacts on the health of Bangkok residents, particularly older people, people with underlying health conditions, outdoor workers and those who are especially vulnerable to heat. BMA is therefore strengthening the city’s preparedness and response through a systematic approach, including heat-risk monitoring and public alerts, cooling spaces, expanded green spaces and targeted support for those most in need of protection. The development of the Heat-Health Action Plan will build on these ongoing efforts by using data and scientific evidence to identify the areas and populations most affected by heat and inform measures tailored to local needs. This will help reduce health impacts and strengthen Bangkok’s long-term resilience to the health risks of a changing climate.”
Extreme heat is a growing public health threat in Bangkok—and it is not felt equally. Older people, outdoor workers, residents of low-income or densely populated communities and people with NCDs—such as heart disease and asthma—face greater risks because of differences in health, occupation, housing, surrounding environments and access to protective services.
The BMA is responding by combining data on heat, health, demographics, occupation and access to heat-protection services to map exposure and vulnerability across the city, strengthen early warning systems and target public health interventions through a dedicated Heat-Health Action Plan.
“Heat risk is not determined by temperature alone. Two communities experiencing similar temperatures can face very different health risks depending on factors such as age, health conditions, occupation, housing and access to cooling and other protective measures,” said Assoc Prof Dr Ekbordin Winijkul, Dean of AIT’s Faculty of Civil and Environmental Engineering. “Our goal is to provide scientific evidence that helps identify not only where it is hottest, but also where heat is most likely to affect people’s health and what interventions can make the greatest difference.”
Mapping heat risk across Bangkok
Low-cost sensors will be used to collect accurate, localised data. Integrated with meteorological, satellite, demographic, health and occupational information, these data will help build assessments of high-risk populations and provide greater visibility to health risks in workplaces, communities and homes.
“Extreme heat magnifies existing inequalities, placing people with the fewest resources and protections at greatest risk,” said Farhad Ali, Deputy Regional Director for Asia Pacific, Partnership for Healthy Cities at Vital Strategies. “This project reflects Bangkok’s commitment to confront the significant public health impacts of extreme heat, transforming local data into targeted action that saves lives.”
Selected high-risk districts will serve as pilot sites for community outreach and risk communication, support for older people and people living with chronic diseases, measures to protect outdoor workers from heat risks and improved access to cooling spaces and drinking water. Lessons will help determine which approaches are practical and responsive to the needs of different communities and inform recommendations for wider implementation across Bangkok.

This year’s El Niño is already breaking records months before reaching peak intensity, with the world’s oceans recording 100 consecutive days of unprecedented heat.
El Niño, a natural warming of the eastern Pacific Ocean that shifts weather patterns globally, is already the third-most intense event on record, according to a new analysis.
The temperature rise at the heart of El Niño in the Pacific reached 3.05C on 19 September, the highest daily reading in 150 years of modern measurements, according to Climate Reanalyzer, using data from the world’s top meteorological agencies. That exceeded the previous high of 3.02C in November 2015 and arrived two months earlier in the calendar year than that previous peak.
The figure is measured against the average sea surface temperature between 1991 and 2020. Another measure, ONI, which uses a rolling 30-year average and accounts for human-caused global warming, shows the event sits just a hundredth of a degree below the 2015 record. Both metrics draw on data from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
Averaged over August, the most recent full month for which data was available, the Niño 3.4 anomaly – a specific point in the Pacific used as a reference for the event as a whole – stood at 2.45C. That’s higher than every previous El Niño on record except the 2015-16 event, which peaked at 2.75C, and a reconstructed 1877-78 event which reached 2.7C based on sparse historical ship data.
El Niño events are classed as “weak” when the Niño 3.4 anomaly reaches 0.5C, “moderate” above 1C, “strong” above 1.5C, and “very strong” above 2.0C, climate scientist Zeke Hausfather explained. “For this year’s event, the Niño 3.4 anomaly has now reached 3.07C, which puts it in a statistical tie with the record set on 18 November 2015, set during a ‘very strong’ El Nino event.”
Averaging 14 seasonal forecast models, Mr Hausfather noted in Carbon Brief, the ongoing event was projected to peak at around 4.1C later this year, about 1.3C above the 2015-16 record.
Each of the 674 individual model runs in the latest analysis predicted a new record would be set. No forecasting system had previously been tested against an El Niño of this scale, he said, because none had occurred.
“The current El Niño event, which has been underway since June and is expected to last until next year, has been developing faster than any previous event on record,” Mr Hausfather wrote.
Sea surface temperatures across the world, outside the polar regions, broke daily records every day between 2 June and 10 September, exceeding readings for the calendar date in any year since 1982, according to the Climate Reanalyzer.
The highest reading of 21.1C came on 22 August, according to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. The Climate Reanalyzer, using data from NOAA, recorded an even higher weekly average of 21.18C in the days that followed.
El Niño is the warm phase of a natural cycle known as the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, which sees trade winds across the tropical Pacific weaken and warm water that normally pools in the western Pacific shift east and rise to the surface.
This raises sea surface temperatures and, with a lag of several months, global air temperatures too. So, most of this event's impact on land is expected to be felt in 2027 rather than this year.
El Nino can have different impacts on different regions. It can increase rainfall in some places and create drought-like conditions in others. This year’s event has been described as a “super El Nino” because of its intensity and existing warming due to the climate crisis.
Zachary Labe, climate scientist at the US-based non-profit Climate Central, told a press briefing on 10 September that the underlying ocean warmth was driven by the human-caused climate crisis, and that more than 90 per cent of the excess heat from burning fossil fuels and greenhouse gas emissions went into the ocean rather than the atmosphere.
"The driver of this record warmth is climate change," he said.
Mr Labe said this heat was not staying near the surface but reaching hundreds of metres deeper, disrupting marine food chains, fisheries and tourism, and adding energy to weather systems like hurricanes.
A UN Environment Programme report found that global temperatures were likely to exceed the 1.5C limit set in the 2015 Paris Agreement within the next few years, the threshold marked by scientists as critical to avoiding the most dangerous effects of the climate crisis.

During the summer months, Newsbook Maltareceived a number of phone calls from prisoners who said they were suffering from extreme heat in their cells because the fans were not coping with the temperatures.
In response to these complaints, the Ministry for Home Affairs and Security told this newsroom that no prisoner had ended up as a patient at Mater Dei Hospital due to health conditions that developed as a result of the heat.
In recent days, reports emerged in the media that a prisoner had died due to the heat in prison. This was denied by Minister Glenn Bedingfield.
Following the Minister’s statement, questions remained regarding the prisoners, particularly in light of the fact that Newsbook Malta had been receiving information for months directly from the Corradino Correctional Facility about the difficulties being experienced by both prisoners and staff due to the heat.
The newsroom therefore asked the Ministry whether any prisoners had suffered health problems due to the heat during the summer months, whether any prisoners had required medical attention, and whether any prisoners had been admitted to hospital because of the heat.
The response consisted of a single sentence stating only that no patient had been admitted to hospital. There was no response regarding health problems caused by the heat.
A prisoner from Division 13 spoke to Newsbook Malta and said that the fan was unable to cope with the heat, to the extent that they spent nights during the summer unable to sleep.
This was in addition to other problems, including allegedly “water that fills you with rust” and cockroaches. Several other prisoners also spoke to us about issues concerning work and payment.
As explained to Newsbook Malta, prisoners who need to purchase medication are allegedly unable to do so because they are never given work and consequently cannot afford the medicines they need as their money does not last. “I will leave here homeless,” one prisoner told us.
Those who are given work in prison allegedly do so for just a few cents a day, with some prisoners receiving 50 cents for distributing milk, bread and other food and cleaning their division. This is in addition to around €9 in VAT allegedly being deducted from their total payment.
“I have no family, I can’t call out for my mother or father,” a prisoner said tearfully. “They are making my life miserable.”
In recent months, we have also received reports of divisions being overcrowded with prisoners, to the extent that they do not even get an opportunity during the day to make a short phone call to their relatives to let them know that they are well.
“My girlfriend was in hospital. I wanted to call her, but I didn’t manage to,” one prisoner said. Call after call has indicated that what is being portrayed outside regarding the reality in prison is completely different from what prisoners say they are actually experiencing.
“What are they playing at with us? They are making fun of you. What kind of things are these?” another prisoner said.

NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WTVF) — Three fires in three days made for a difficult stretch for DeKalb County’s volunteer firefighters, who spent hours battling flames and extreme heat over the weekend.
Several firefighters needed treatment at the scene, but no one was taken to the hospital.
The latest fire broke out Saturday at a barn that once housed an antique store. DeKalb County Fire Chief Donny Green said the store had been closed, but the building still held memories for people in the community.
“People from out of town would come there and stop by, and lots of memories there from the community,” Green said.
When firefighters arrived Saturday, Green said flames had already taken over much of the structure. An old farmhouse was just feet away.
“When we got there the flames were already leaking up the house and melted the vinyl siding off the house,” Green said.
Crews were able to keep the fire from destroying the nearby home.
The response came during an already exhausting stretch for the county’s volunteer firefighters. Green said crews had responded to another fire Thursday and spent about four hours Friday afternoon battling another fire in intense heat.
By Saturday, firefighters were once again working in high temperatures while wearing protective gear designed to shield them from the flames.
“It protects you from heat but it also holds in heat, so it was challenging for our volunteers and I’m proud of them,” Green said.
The conditions took a toll. Green said some firefighters required IV treatment for dehydration, while another firefighter suffered a minor burn and was treated at the scene.
“We had firefighters that had to have IV treatment for dehydration and one firefighter that had a minor burn also treated on the scene,” Green said.
Community members also stepped in to help firefighters during the demanding stretch.
“They wanted to do what they can do to help. They brought us water and their side-by-sides out and transporting our firefighters,” Green said.
DeKalb County’s 82 firefighters are all volunteers and are spread across 12 remote stations. Green said serving their neighbors is what motivates many of them to give up their time.
“Making a difference and making a difference for your neighbors is what drives most of these people to do what they do,” Green said.
No one was taken to the hospital following the fires.
Green said the department has also been recognized at the state level for its training.
The cause of Saturday’s barn fire remains undetermined.
